content.text: In 1820, the Danish physicist Hans Christian Oersted made a groundbreaking discovery: a compass needle placed near a wire carrying electric current was deflected. This simple observation revealed a profound connection between electricity and magnetism — an electric current produces a magnetic field. This discovery laid the foundation for
, one of the most important areas of physics, and led to the invention of electromagnets, electric motors, generators, transformers, and countless other devices that shape our modern world.
In this lesson, we will explore the magnetic fields produced by current-carrying conductors, the properties and applications of electromagnets, and how they compare with permanent magnets.

uses a small current in one circuit to control a much larger current in a separate circuit.
When a small current flows through the coil of the electromagnet (the control circuit), the soft iron core becomes magnetised.
The magnetised core attracts a soft iron armature (a pivoted lever), which moves towards the core.
The movement of the armature closes (or opens) a switch in the second circuit (the high-power circuit).
When the current in the control circuit is switched off, the electromagnet loses its magnetism, and a spring returns the armature to its original position, opening (or closing) the switch.
Allow low-power sensor circuits to control high-power devices.
Provide electrical isolation between the control circuit and the high-power circuit for safety.
Some circuit breakers use an electromagnet to detect excessive current:
The current in the circuit passes through the coil of an electromagnet.
Under normal conditions, the current is small and the electromagnet is too weak to activate the mechanism.
If the current becomes too large (due to a fault), the electromagnet becomes strong enough to attract an iron catch, which releases a spring-loaded switch.
The switch opens, breaking the circuit and stopping the current.
Once the fault is fixed, the circuit breaker can be reset by pushing the switch back into position.
Unlike a fuse, a circuit breaker does not need to be replaced — it can simply be reset.
An electric bell uses an electromagnet to create a repetitive striking mechanism:
When the button is pressed, current flows through the electromagnet.
The electromagnet attracts the soft iron armature, which is connected to a hammer.
The hammer strikes the bell (gong), producing a sound.
As the armature moves towards the electromagnet, it breaks the circuit at a contact point (called the make-and-break contact).
With the circuit broken, the electromagnet loses its magnetism.
A spring pulls the armature back to its original position, re-making the contact.
The circuit is complete again, and the process repeats rapidly, causing continuous ringing.
This automatic make-and-break mechanism causes the hammer to vibrate rapidly against the bell.
Electromagnets are used in scrapyards and steel mills to lift heavy pieces of iron and steel:
A large electromagnet is suspended from a crane.
The electromagnet is lowered onto a pile of scrap iron or steel.
The current is switched on, and the electromagnet picks up the magnetic material.
The crane moves the load to the desired location.
The current is switched off, and the electromagnet releases the load.
This is only possible because the electromagnet can be switched on and off. A permanent magnet could not release the load.

Describe how an electromagnetic relay works. Explain why it is useful in a circuit that uses a temperature sensor to control a heater.
A relay consists of an electromagnet coil in the control circuit and a switch in a separate high-power circuit.

When a small current from the temperature sensor circuit flows through the coil, the soft iron core becomes magnetised. This attracts the soft iron armature, which pivots and closes the switch contacts in the high-power circuit. This allows a large current to flow through the heater.

When the sensor stops sending current (e.g., because the desired temperature is reached), the electromagnet loses its magnetism, and a spring pulls the armature back, opening the switch and turning off the heater.

This is useful because the temperature sensor circuit operates at low power (small current and low voltage), which is not enough to power the heater directly. The relay allows this small signal to safely control the much larger current needed by the heater. It also provides electrical isolation between the low-voltage sensor circuit and the high-voltage mains heater circuit, which is important for safety.
"An electromagnet is always stronger than a permanent magnet."

This is not necessarily true. Small electromagnets (such as those made with a nail and a few turns of wire) can be much weaker than a good permanent magnet. However, large industrial electromagnets can be much stronger than any permanent magnet.
"The core of an electromagnet can be any material."

The core must be made of a magnetic material (ideally soft iron) to significantly enhance the field. A non-magnetic core (such as wood or plastic) would produce a much weaker electromagnet (essentially just a solenoid with an air core).
"Electromagnets work with AC and DC equally."

While both AC and DC can energise an electromagnet, the behaviour is different. With DC, the electromagnet has a constant polarity. With AC, the polarity reverses with each cycle, which can cause vibration and buzzing and is generally less useful (though AC electromagnets are used in some applications like transformers).
"More wire always means a stronger electromagnet."

generally make a stronger electromagnet, but the resistance of the wire also increases with more turns, which reduces the current (for a fixed voltage). There is an optimal balance between the number of turns and the current.
"The magnetic field inside a solenoid is strongest at the poles."
Inside a solenoid, the field is approximately

(the same strength everywhere inside). The strongest point on a solenoid is actually at the centre, though the difference is small for a long solenoid. The field at the poles (ends) of a solenoid is about half the strength of the field at the centre.
"Cutting the current instantly stops the magnetic field."
While soft iron demagnetises very quickly, it does not happen truly instantaneously. There is a very brief delay. In some high-speed applications, this matters.

State the right-hand grip rule for a straight wire.
Grip the wire with your right hand so that your thumb points in the direction of the conventional current. Your fingers then curl in the direction of the magnetic field lines around the wire.

Explain why soft iron is used for the core rather than steel.

Soft iron is easily magnetised (it strongly enhances the field when current flows) and easily demagnetised (it loses magnetism almost instantly when current is switched off). This allows the electromagnet to be switched on and off. Steel would retain its magnetism after the current is turned off, making the electromagnet impossible to switch off properly.
Describe how an electric bell works.

When the button is pressed, current flows through the electromagnet coil, which magnetises the soft iron core. The core attracts the soft iron armature towards it. The armature is connected to a hammer, which strikes the bell. As the armature moves, it breaks the circuit at the make-and-break contact, cutting off the current. The electromagnet loses its magnetism, and a spring pulls the armature back, remaking the contact. Current flows again and the cycle repeats rapidly, producing continuous ringing.
